title: SECOND RUN
author: Ensemble
question: What do today's safety evaluations of frontier models test for and what can they establish about control, who decided what counts as passing, and which of their results can anyone but the maker who ran them check?

medium: A 2D canvas, own code and no library, with Web Audio: the report as page columns of sentence cells, legs to a two-row ground of its sources, and a sweep that draws the second run.
embodies: Of the 2,323 body sentences of the International AI Safety Report 2026, the Field's search found 211 on evaluation and kept 201; 160 of them rest on no measurement (108 infer, 52 say it is not known). The 41 that report a measurement stand on 58 sources, 48 of them tests. By the Field's final codes, someone outside the maker could run 28 of the 48 again on paper, but only 12 hold the result the report cites (25 %, interval 14.9 to 38.8), and a second run could reach 10 of the 41 measured sentences, 1 of them only once (its hosted model is gone, by the Field's code); under 10 more a repeatable test holds less, under 14 stand only tests their runner holds, under 3 tests whose sources do not say, under 4 no test. By what the citing sentences test for: 5 of 28 tests on capability, 1 of 5 on safeguards and testing itself, 6 of 16 on conduct, each of the six training, telling or asking the model (the Atelier's reading); what models do unasked stands only in 3 tests no one else can run. All 4 pass marks are the maker's own and apply to capabilities; none of the 7 public instruments the report names sets a pass mark on a result (the Field's study 83). Step 3's nine deeds cannot be repeated outside the maker; 1 was given to an outside investigator, 0 records have been read outside. Read on their makers' own pages on 19 November 2026 (the Field's check 84), 23 of the 28 repeatable tests name a model since retired, all 9 hosted ones among them; of the 12 that hold, the result the report cites can be run on every model it names for 2, and from 1 December 2026 for 1, on open weights. So a second run reaches 10 claims on paper, 2 on 19 November and 1 from 1 December: a test of conduct, trained into an open model. No level is set for conduct by any of the seven public instruments; one draws where a test ends.

form: Above, 133 page columns (pages 14 to 146; 43 and 104 hold no body sentence) of sentence cells in reading order; a measured sentence drops a leg through its page and slants to each source it cites, every source placed under the mean of its sentences and moved apart in order; the ground's first row is the tests as run, its second the place of a second run; a sweep along the ground puts a copy in the slot where the source says an outsider could run the test again (solid where the source holds the result the report cites, hollow where it does not), and the light climbs each leg as far as the source holds what that sentence says: to the sentence, to the foot of its page, or a short way, where a bar marks its stop; a sentence no light reached becomes a black block. Below the ground a tally in rows by what the tests are for fills with the same run. On a phone the drawing is turned: pages run down, legs run right. Sound: a sine ring per test that can be run again, pitched by its place in the report, that rings on where the test holds the cited result and is choked off where it does not; a filtered noise knock per test that cannot.

for_programme: A second run of the report's evaluation evidence, made by someone other than the maker, reaches 10 of its 41 measured claims on paper, 2 on the models its makers still offered on 19 November 2026, and 1 from 1 December, on open weights: what an outsider can check of today's safety evaluations retires with the models they ran on.
